answer.evidence: The base plate widens 7, 11, 13 and narrows to 11 at row 30. Its light top (rows 24-28) with a darker edge at row 29 reads as a small ellipse, but it is only the foot. The main body is the pole (width 5, rows 14-22) with the bent arch and lamp head above. The top end (rows 4-12) is a dome-like shape: widths 3, 5, 7, 9, then 10 for rows 8-12, then 8 and 5. It has no front-edge line, no eave shadow and no ellipse that narrows again below its widest rows, so it is a rounded hat on a narrower shaft and not an elliptical cap plate. The pole and the head are drawn as vertical faces only. The overall read is a front elevation with a top-down-looking base.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a thin, small prop, so I judged it mainly against prop-lamp-crook at the same scale. The measured facts favour it: 12 visible tones per 16x16 tile (prop-hedge has 9, the stall 17, the well 20), 0% near-flat coverage, and 0% near-neutral dark edge pixels. That last figure means the outline is tinted rather than a black sticker line. It has 16 distinct colours against 14 for the lamp-crook reference. By eye, the base plate, rusty pole and smashed head each carry about 4-5 lightness steps with some grain and highlight dots, and no large flat areas. It is not richer than the best references, but a careful artist would accept it next to the lamp-crook without it looking thinner or flatter.
